newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa to step up gasoline imports in 1997.
newsitem.headline: South Africa to step up gasoline imports in 1997.

text.p: Imports of gasoline are likely to become more common in South Africa this year while exports tail off as domestic refining capacity and demand reach virtual equilibrium, industry sources said.

According to the South African Petroleum Industry Association, the country last year had the capacity to produce 12.3 billion litres of gasoline against estimated demand of 11.4 billion litres. Demand in 1995 was 10.1 billion litres.
But refineries did not run at full capacity all the time and small parcels of imports were needed increasingly from the middle of last year.

With domestic consumption growing at between five and six percent a year, demand is likely to top 12 billion litres this year and gasoline imports are expected to become more common, although still a small percentage of total demand.
Statistics provided by the department of mineral and energy affairs reflect this rising trend.

In 1995, South Africa imported 126.6 million litres of gasoline and exported just over a billion litres. In the first nine months of 1996, it imported 430.6 million litres and exported 677 million litres, indicating a fall-off in gasoline exports as local demand picked up.
In response, oil-from-coal producer Sasol Ltd has been re-engineering its Secunda plant and is expected to be able to produce more synthetic fuel to help meet growing local demand.

But plans by other oil companies such as Royal Dutch/Shell and BP to expand refinery capacity have been placed on hold as they await finalisation of the government's plans to deregulate or re-regulate the tightly controlled industry.
Engen and Caltex, meanwhile, told Reuters that they had sufficient capacity to meet demand for the next few years but were continually fine-tuning their plants to improve yields.

Although supply and demand for gasoline are reaching equilibrium, diesel and gas oil supplies still outstrip demand and supplies are being exported. Nine billion litres of diesel were produced last year while demand was seven billion litres. Diesel exports totalled 2.3 billion litres in 1995 and 1.6 billion litres in the first nine months of 1996.

The bias in favour of gasoline in South Africa has prompted the department of transport to investigate the possibility of switching mass transport vehicles such as minibus taxis from gasoline to diesel.

Caltex supply and trading manager Kevin Mulder said it would not make economic sense to add to refining capacity just yet because of low refining margins, regulatory uncertainty and the fact that most of the product would have to be exported.
Sasol spokesman Alfonso Niemand agreed, saying that any new refinery built in South Africa would have to be a world class one with a capacity of between 150,000 and 200,000 barrels a day.

"Such a refinery would have to have its base load in the local market and therefore will probably only be built by about 2005 because you can't build a refinery and then find you have to export 95 percent of the production because local demand is not sufficient," Niemand said.

Imports would be needed until local demand justified a new refinery. Industry sources said the most likely sources were the Middle East, where several new refineries were coming on stream and there was surplus capacity.
South Africa last year had a surplus of most fuel products, but a slight shortfall of fuel oil, which is expected to increase as refineries maximise their white products output.
The country has two crude oil refineries in Durban, one in Cape Town and one in the interior, plus Sasol's oil-from-coal facilities at Secunda.
